present.explain: A Russian verb's ending says who does it: я пью (I drink), ты пьёшь (you drink), он пьёт (he drinks); я чита́ю, ты чита́ешь, она́ чита́ет; я иду́, ты идёшь, мы идём, вы идёте. Learn each verb's forms as you meet them: пить and идти́ change more than their ending.
present.why: English changes its verb only for he and she; Russian changes it for everyone, so [[пью]] already says I drink. The same form says I drink and I'm drinking: Russian has no -ing.

examples.text: Мы идём домой, а он читает.
examples.means: We're going home, and he's reading.
examples.literal: We go home, and he reads.

contrasts.says: English adds -s only for he and she, and says I'm drinking with -ing; Russian has one form for both, with an ending for each person.
After хочу́ or могу́, the next verb takes no ending: Я хочу́ пить.

mistakes.why: With я, it's пью.
With ты, it's чита́ешь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every Russian noun is a он word, a она́ word or an оно́ word, and the words with it match: оди́н чай, одна́ маши́на; мой телефо́н, моя́ маши́на. Most nouns ending in a consonant are он words (телефо́н, ключ, дом), most ending in -а are она́ words (су́мка, маши́на, ма́ма), and most ending in -о are оно́ words (молоко́). ко́фе is a он word though it ends in -е.
gender.why: English has he, she and it for people and for what you point back to; Russian sorts every noun this way, so a phone is он: Где телефо́н? [[Он]] здесь. Learn which with the word; the ending usually tells you.

examples.means: My coffee is on the table.

contrasts.says: English calls a thing it; Russian calls a телефо́н он and a су́мка она́, as it would a man and a woman.
мой and твой follow the noun's gender: мой ключ, моя́ су́мка.

mistakes.why: телефо́н is a он word: мой.
чай is a он word: оди́н.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

no-be.explain: In the present, Russian says no am, is or are: Я до́ма (I'm at home), Телефо́н на столе́ (the phone is on the table), Где ключ? (where's the key?). The words just stand side by side.
no-be.why: English needs a verb in every sentence; Russian leaves to be out in the present, as an English headline does (Phone on table).

contrasts.says: English can't leave is out (The phone on the table isn't a sentence); Russian always does in the present.
Э́то alone says this is: Э́то мой ключ (this my key).

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes/no question keeps a statement's order; only the voice rises on the word asked about (the ? when written): Маши́на здесь. (the car's here) → Маши́на здесь? (is the car here?). A question word (где, что, чей) most often comes first: Где маши́на? Что ты чита́ешь?
question.why: English turns words around or adds do (Do you drink coffee?); Russian changes nothing but the voice: Ты пьёшь ко́фе? There's no do in Russian at all.

contrasts.says: English moves is or adds do (Is the car here? Do you read?); Russian keeps the order and lets the voice ask.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

accusative.explain: What you drink, read or hold takes the accusative. For она́ words ending in -а, the -а becomes -у: вода́ → Я пью во́ду, кни́га → Я чита́ю кни́гу, газе́та → Он чита́ет газе́ту. он and оно́ words stay as they are: Я пью чай, Я пью молоко́.
accusative.why: English shows who does what by order alone; Russian also marks it on the word, so [[во́ду]] is water as what's drunk, wherever it stands.

contrasts.says: English never changes water for what you drink; Russian does: вода́, во́ду.
Where something is takes -е instead: в маши́не, на столе́.

mistakes.why: What you drink: во́ду.
What he reads: кни́гу.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

prepositional.explain: After в (in) and на (on, at), where something is takes the prepositional, mostly ending in -е: стол → на столе́, су́мка → в су́мке, маши́на → в маши́не, рабо́та → на рабо́те.
prepositional.why: English says where with in and on alone; Russian says it twice, with the little word and with the ending, so [[столе́]] after на is the table as a place.

examples.means: The key is on the table.
The phone is in the bag.

contrasts.says: English's on and in change nothing after them; Russian's change the word.
до́ма (at home) and домо́й (home, going there) say it without в or на.

mistakes.why: After в, where it is: су́мке.
After на, where she is: рабо́те.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: мой (my) and твой (your) match their noun as an adjective does: мой телефо́н, моя́ су́мка; твой ключ, твоя́ маши́на. твой is for someone you say ты to.
possessive.why: English's my never changes; Russian's follows the noun's gender, so [[моя́]] tells you су́мка is a она́ word.

examples.means: Your bag is on the table.

contrasts.says: The noun's gender decides: мой for он words, моя́ for она́ words.
English has one my; Russian has мой and моя́, and more forms you'll meet.

mistakes.why: ключ is a он word: мой.
су́мка is a она́ word: твоя́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

short-adjective.explain: A few adjectives have a short form for how someone is, and it says the gender: гото́в (a man), гото́ва (a woman), гото́вы (more than one, or вы). Я гото́в. Она́ гото́ва. Мы гото́вы.
short-adjective.why: English's ready is the same for everyone; Russian's says who it's about, so a woman says Я [[гото́ва]] and a man Я гото́в.

contrasts.says: English says ready for anyone; Russian's form says a man, a woman or more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's гото́вы.

mistakes.why: With мы: гото́вы.
With она́: гото́ва.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

direction.explain: Being somewhere and going there are different words: до́ма is at home, домо́й is home as where you go: Я до́ма (I'm at home), Я иду́ домо́й (I'm going home).
direction.why: English uses home for both; Russian asks where at or where to. A verb of going takes [[домо́й]]; being, drinking or reading there takes до́ма.

contrasts.says: English's home is both; Russian's до́ма is where you are and домо́й where you go.
идти́ (to go) takes домо́й: Я иду́ домо́й.

mistakes.why: Where you are: до́ма.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

ne.explain: не goes right before the word it denies, most often the verb: Я не пью ко́фе (I don't drink coffee), Я не могу́ помо́чь (I can't help). Russian has no do: не alone says don't.
ne.why: English needs do to say not (I don't drink); Russian puts [[не]] in front of the verb and changes nothing else.

contrasts.says: English adds do or does (I don't, she doesn't); Russian never does.
With nothing to have, нет takes есть's place: У меня́ нет рабо́ты.

mistakes.why: Before a verb it's не; нет is no.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

infinitive.explain: After хочу́ (I want), могу́ (I can) and дава́й (let's), the next verb stays in its dictionary form: Я хочу́ пить, Я могу́ помо́чь, Дава́й пить чай.
infinitive.why: English says to after want (I want to drink) and nothing after can; Russian needs neither: the dictionary form, like [[пить]], does it.

contrasts.says: Only the first verb takes the ending: Я хочу́ пить.
English adds to after want; Russian adds nothing.

mistakes.why: After хочу́, the dictionary form: пить.
After могу́: помо́чь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

have.explain: To say you have something, Russian says it's at you: У меня́ есть рабо́та (at me is work: I have work), У тебя́ есть маши́на? (do you have a car?). With none, нет takes есть's place, and the thing takes the genitive: У меня́ нет рабо́ты.
have.why: English's have is a verb of its own; Russian builds it from у (at) and меня́ (me), so У меня́ есть is I have, and the thing you have is the sentence's subject.

examples.means: I still have work to do.

contrasts.says: English's have is a verb; Russian says the thing is at you.
With нет, the thing takes the genitive: рабо́та becomes рабо́ты.

mistakes.why: What you have stays as it is: рабо́та.
After у, я becomes меня́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: э́тот (this) matches its noun: э́тот телефо́н, э́та су́мка. э́то on its own says this is or that's, with no is, and never changes: Э́то мой ключ, Э́то су́мка ма́мы.
demonstrative.why: English says this for both; Russian's э́тот points at a thing and matches it, and э́то presents one: Э́то [[маши́на]] ма́мы (this is Mom's car).

contrasts.says: After its noun, мой or моя́ alone says mine: Э́тот телефо́н мой.
Э́то alone says this is.

mistakes.why: су́мка is a она́ word: э́та.
телефо́н is a он word: э́тот.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

address.explain: ты is for one person you know well; вы is for someone you don't know well, or for more than one, and takes the plural verb form: Ты идёшь домо́й? to a friend, Вы идёте домо́й? to a stranger or to two friends.
address.why: English has one you; Russian chooses, and the verb's ending follows: вы [[идёте]].

contrasts.says: English's you is one word for everyone; Russian's says how well you know them, or that there's more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's гото́вы.

mistakes.why: With вы: идёте.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

question-word.explain: Кто asks who, что what, где where, куда́ where to, отку́да where from, когда́ when and почему́ why. Usually start with the question word. Either the subject or the verb can follow: Куда́ ты идёшь? Куда́ идёт твой друг? Both orders are normal. If кто itself is the subject, the verb is singular: Кто стучи́т? A question about a place needs no is: Где ключ?
question-word.why: English often adds do or moves an auxiliary before the subject. Russian adds no do: Что ты и́щешь? The question word says what information is missing. Where has three useful counterparts: где for a location, куда́ for a destination, отку́да for a starting point.

contrasts.says: English often changes the order and adds do. Russian uses its ordinary verb form: Что ты чита́ешь?
Где asks about a location, as in Где твой дом? Куда́ asks about a destination, as in Куда́ ты идёшь? Отку́да asks about a starting point.
Ты стучи́шь? asks for yes or no. Кто стучи́т? asks for the person. Question words can also come later for emphasis or a follow-up: Ты куда́?

mistakes.why: When кто is the subject, use the third-person singular стучи́т, even when asking the listener who is knocking.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

pronoun-object.explain: When a pronoun names the person heard or seen, it takes its accusative form: я → меня́, ты → тебя́, он → его́, она́ → её, мы → нас, вы → вас, они́ → их. Ты меня́ слы́шишь? means Can you hear me? Я тебя́ ви́жу means I can see you. These forms often come before the verb; they can come after it too. The verb still agrees with the subject: я слы́шу, ты слы́шишь, она́ слы́шит.
pronoun-object.why: English changes I to me and he to him. Russian changes you too: ты becomes тебя́ when someone hears or sees you. The ending tells you the role even when the order changes: Ты меня́ слы́шишь? and Ты слы́шишь меня́? can both ask Can you hear me?

contrasts.says: English normally puts me after hear. Russian often puts меня́ before слы́шишь. Neither position is compulsory in Russian.
For the person heard or seen, use тебя́: Я тебя́ ви́жу. For the person receiving help, use тебе́: Я могу́ тебе́ помо́чь. Learn the form with the verb.
Use тебя́ with a friend you call ты. Use вас for someone you call вы, whether one person politely or several people.

mistakes.why: The person heard is the direct object: меня́, not the dative мне.
The person seen takes тебя́, not the dative тебе́.
Она́ is a subject form; the woman heard takes её.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.
